nodes.label: FastAPI service layer design note (PYQ-213)
nodes.rationale: Kept as-is after implementation (PYQ-261) because the implementation followed it directly; this page is the reasoning, http-api.md is the interface.

nodes.label: Additive second front-end, not a rewrite
nodes.rationale: The analysis/model/data layers are already fully decoupled from Typer/Rich and cli/app.py is a thin caller over plain functions returning plain dataclasses, so a FastAPI app wraps exactly those same functions and nothing in the core has to move.

nodes.label: pyquant/api/ package layout
nodes.rationale: app.py / schemas.py / deps.py / jobs.py / routes/, behind an optional api extra so the base install stays lean.

nodes.label: Pydantic response models at the API boundary
nodes.rationale: Numpy is the sharp edge: every np.ndarray/np.float64 must be converted or JSON encoding fails, so conversion is centralized at the boundary and the API contract stays decoupled from internal dataclass changes.

nodes.label: Shared serializers between CLI and API (PYQ-212 first)
nodes.rationale: Implement domain-to-JSON-able-dict functions once, have the CLI print them and the API return them; build PYQ-212 first so numpy-to-JSON logic is never duplicated, then wrap in thin pydantic models purely for OpenAPI schema generation.

nodes.label: Training as a background job (202 + job id)
nodes.rationale: tft.train() blocks for a full Lightning fit - seconds on synthetic data, minutes or longer on real 5y panels - so a request thread must not block on it.

nodes.label: In-process job registry (v1 scaffold)
nodes.rationale: A dict[str, JobRecord] guarded by a lock, updated by the background task on completion - good enough for one instance and low training concurrency.

nodes.label: Triggers to graduate to a real job queue
nodes.rationale: Job state in process memory is lost on restart and invisible to a second instance; no concurrency control means two large fits can OOM; no retries, backpressure, scheduling or cancellation; BackgroundTasks shares the event loop so a CPU-bound fit needs a worker pool anyway. Move to arq or Celery+Redis the moment you need durable jobs, more than one instance, or bounded training concurrency.

nodes.label: Bundle storage backend decision (local disk vs object storage)
nodes.rationale: Multi-instance breaks local disk: the box that served POST /train is not necessarily the one serving GET /forecast later. Prerequisites regardless of backend are PYQ-220 (absolute checkpoint/cache paths - a server's CWD is not the repo root) and a load_bundle/save_bundle abstraction so local-vs-S3 is one swap rather than scattered Path joins.

nodes.label: Measured forecast latency profile (PYQ-319)
nodes.rationale: AAPL, default period=5y: cold total ~65.4 s of which fetch+panel-build is 64.3 s (98%); predict() is 812 ms cold / 632 ms warm; warm total ~0.84 s. Caveat: one symbol, one run, live vendor latency at 2026-07-27 - the qualitative conclusion is robust, the millisecond figures are not.

nodes.label: Panel cache hit rate decides perceived service latency
nodes.rationale: The forward pass is not the bottleneck. The LRU bundle cache saves ~250-450 ms; a panel cache or background pre-warm saves ~64 s. FRED's 15 requests per cold call at the default period means an operator serving many distinct symbols cold hits the FRED rate limit long before CPU or GPU does.

nodes.label: Per-bundle prediction lock (design)
nodes.rationale: TemporalFusionTransformer.predict() is not safe to call concurrently on the same model instance - pytorch-forecasting spins up an internal Lightning Trainer per call and mutates model state. Serialize per model; parallelism across different bundles is fine, and torch intra-op threading already uses multiple cores so the cost is lower than it sounds.

nodes.label: In-process LRU cache of ModelBundle (design)
nodes.rationale: Reloading per request pays checkpoint deserialization every time and re-triggers the weights_only=False unpickle (PYQ-306). Bounded size caps memory; entries are invalidated when the bundle is retrained.

nodes.label: Long-running server is where schema drift bites (PYQ-302)
nodes.rationale: 'Source enabled at train time, rate-limited at predict time' is exactly the server case; unresolved, a transient upstream outage yields malformed predictions rather than a clean error. The design also depends on the FinBERT cache fix (PYQ-114), which memoizes only on success so a transient first-request failure no longer disables sentiment for the process lifetime.

nodes.label: API-key gate as a FastAPI dependency (design)
nodes.rationale: A public endpoint would spend the operator's FRED/Finnhub/Yahoo quota on every caller. Keys from config/secret store, constant-time compare, 401 on failure; never echo upstream API keys in responses or logs.

nodes.label: Per-key rate limiting (deferred)
nodes.rationale: Training especially must be tightly capped since it is expensive and quota-hungry; slowapi or the reverse-proxy/API-gateway layer are the candidate places.

nodes.label: Deployment shape (CPU image for serving, CUDA for training)
nodes.rationale: A CPU-only image is enough for forecast/explain/scan; training wants CUDA. Built via uv sync --frozen --extra api, entry point uvicorn pyquant.api.app:app. Pairs with PYQ-217.

nodes.label: Recommended API build order
nodes.rationale: Serializers (PYQ-212) then absolute paths (PYQ-220) before any endpoint, read-only endpoints before /train, Dockerfile before deploy, and object storage plus a Redis queue only if and when multi-instance or durability is actually needed.

hyperedges.label: Two front-ends over one serializer/dataclass implementation
